name: Hassan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt for a living. I run a D11 dozer at Black Range, a big open-cut coal mine, mostly ripping and pushing overburden, which is the rock on top of the coal. Day shift starts at six with a pre-start on the machine and a talk with the pit supervisor. I love when a bench comes out clean and flat, and I hate the dust in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work? Home, money, that kind of thing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ama, she's an environmental scientist with the water authority, which makes for some fun dinner talk about coal. We've got about nine months of savings and an index fund I add to every pay. I use AI every day, for planning my study, checking my super, even translating the Japanese manual for the new GPS kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but it doesn't change the bigger problem, which is that coal's on its way out anyway. I'd post that the real transition we need is energy, not chatbots. People at work would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the real clock is the mine's closure plan, which says 2035. AI flopping doesn't change that, and honestly I agree the coal should stop. So I'm still planning my exit, just without a robot pushing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up the drone survey work I've started on the side, and keep putting money in the index fund. I'd start looking at solar farm and pumped hydro builds, because they need dozer operators too. I'd keep using AI for my study plans like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI, about the closure date sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you square loving the dozer with wanting the coal to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I love the dozer, not the coal. A dozer pushing dirt for a pumped hydro dam is the same seat. I just want my seat somewhere that'll still exist in 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ama think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's pushing me to apply to the hydro project out west already. I tell her I'll go when they're hiring operators, not just engineers. We argue about timing, never about the direction.

say: I'd say the transition we really need is **energy, not chatbots**.
I'd point out that **coal is ending** anyway, with or without AI.
think: My real clock is the mine's **2035 closure plan**, which I actually agree with.
I'm still **planning my exit**, just without a robot pushing me.
do: Keep building my **drone survey** side work on weekends.
Keep adding to the **index fund** every pay.
Look for dozer work on **solar and pumped hydro** builds.
feel: A little **uneasy**, because the **closure date** still sits there.
S0.quote: I love the dozer, not the coal. A dozer pushing dirt for a pumped hydro dam is the same seat.
fieldNote: His existing pressure is the mine's **planned closure**, which AI Plateau does nothing to change.
Progressive views and his job pull apart, and he resolves it as **machine, not coal**.
Already uses AI daily and runs a **drone side business**, so he's well positioned.

steps.text: Keep running weekend drone surveys for local farms
Add to the index fund every payday
Apply for dozer work on solar and hydro builds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make mining safer and less dusty, if workers get a say. Remote-controlled dozers already exist, and I'd want the union to make sure operators get those seats. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks good for me. The planning and survey software gets smarter, and that's my side business, so I'd learn it first. Robots come slowly to the pit, and by then I'd want to be the person running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the remote operations course the moment it's offered and keep the AI survey tools sharp. I'd offer to trial anything new on our crew. I'd also keep pushing the hydro project applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, even a bit excited. It's like being offered the next machine before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Kev, who's been on dozers thirty years and still prints his rosters. He'd hate a screen in his cab. I'd sit with him on the tablet stuff, because he taught me to read a bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound excited. Is there any part of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit where the company uses it to cut crews instead of making jobs better. I'd keep an eye on that. A remote dozer is safer for me, but I don't want my safer seat to be the only seat left.

say: I'd say AI could make mining **safer and less dusty** if workers get a say.
I'd want the **union** to secure remote seats for current operators.
think: Smarter **survey software** helps my side business, so I'd learn it first.
By the time robots arrive, I want to be the one **running them**.
do: Sign up for the **remote operations course** as soon as it's offered.
Volunteer my crew to **trial new tools** first.
Keep applying to the **hydro project** out west.
feel: **Calm**, even a little **excited**, like getting the next machine early.
S1.quote: A remote dozer is safer for me, but I don't want my safer seat to be the only seat left.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as **good for him**: new tools feed his survey work.
His worry is for others, especially **Old Kev**, a thirty-year operator who prints rosters.
Progressive streak shows in wanting the **union** to secure remote seats, not just for himself.

steps.text: Enrol in the remote dozer operations course
Trial the new AI survey tools on the crew
Push the union to reserve remote seats for operators
Keep applying to the western hydro project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to treat this like a war footing: public jobs, paid retraining and a share of the profits for workers. I'd be all over social media with it. Ama would probably help me write the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the survey side business dies first, because AGI does surveys and plans by 2028. Then the dozer goes by 2031, remote seat or not, because one robot supervisor watches ten machines. I'm young and I've got money, but I'd have to reinvent myself twice in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop the drone business and sell the gear while it's worth something. I'd put that money and some savings into an electrical apprenticeship, because robots need power and wiring. I'd ask the union to bargain for training paid on full wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lost, I'd have a plan by the end of the week, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you lose if the drone business goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six grand a year and the thing I'm proudest of. I built it myself, my own little logo on the van. Selling the drones would sting more than losing the dozer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ama change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about a wedding next year, a big one. I think we'd go small and put the money aside. Her job checking river samples is mostly hands-on fieldwork, so she might have a few more years than me.

say: I'd call for **public jobs**, paid retraining and a profit share for workers.
I'd post about it constantly, with my girlfriend helping **write the posts**.
think: My **survey business** dies first, by 2028, because AGI does planning.
The **dozer goes by 2031**, so I'd reinvent myself twice in five years.
do: Sell the **drone gear** in the first month while it still has value.
Fund an **electrical apprenticeship** with that money and some savings.
Shrink the **wedding** and set the money aside.
feel: **Anxious**, though he'd have a **plan** within a week.
S2.quote: Selling the drones would sting more than losing the dozer.
fieldNote: Both his incomes are exposed: the **thinking side** in 2028, the **dozer** in 2031.
Adaptability shows as **speed**: he'd sell assets and retrain within weeks.
Losing his **own business** hurts more than losing the employer's machine.

steps.text: Sell the drone survey gear while it still has value
Start an electrical apprenticeship funded from savings
Push the union for training on full wages
Swap the big wedding for a small one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exactly enough time to plan a fair transition, and I'd say it loudly. Mining towns need a plan with dates and money in it. I'd go to the community forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years lines up almost exactly with the coal closure. That's weirdly helpful, because I was already planning to leave in about that time. The robots in 2034 would hit a mine that's closing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship next year, while keeping the dozer job part of the time. I'd steer the drone business towards inspection work on wind turbines and solar farms. I'd use AI tools to keep my study on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly like I've got my timeline confirmed. I was already halfway out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your crew in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them want to stay till the closure, then take the payout. The young ones I'd drag along to the trade school info night. I'd be the annoying one handing out flyers in the crib room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel guilty at all being ready when others aren't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. But being ready means I can help, like sitting with Old Kev on the forms. If I'm drowning too, I'm no use to anyone on my crew.

I'd push for a mining town plan with **dates and money**.
think: AGI by 2031 lines up with the **coal closure**, which helps my timing.
Robots in **2034** would hit a mine that's closing anyway.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** next year while still running the dozer part-time.
Steer the drone business towards **wind and solar inspections**.
Use **AI tools** to keep my study on track.
feel: A little **uneasy**, but mostly **confirmed** in his timeline.
S3.quote: If I'm drowning too, I'm no use to anyone on my crew.
fieldNote: The scenario matches his existing **exit plan**, so the extra years ease him.
He plans to help colleagues, seeing his **readiness** as a duty, not a gloat.
He pivots the drone work to **renewables inspection** rather than abandoning it.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship while working the dozer part-time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get the energy transition and the AI transition right together. I'd push for that at every forum. I'd sound like a broken record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal closes in 2035, before AGI even lands. So by 2039 I'd already be somewhere else, probably wiring robots or running a renewables crew. It actually feels like a good decade for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the dozer until the closure payout, finish the electrical trade by 2030, and grow the inspection business. Keep investing in the index fund. Maybe buy a block of land with Ama somewhere near the hydro project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the future I was already heading towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the closure payout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put most of it on the land, the rest into the business. A van, better drones, a thermal camera. It'd be my start-up money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want governments to do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund apprenticeships for every coal worker who wants one, with a living wage. I can afford to retrain because I saved, but most coal workers can't. Ten years is wasted if only people like me get ready.

say: I'd say ten years lets us get **energy and AI** transitions right together.
I'd repeat it at **every forum**, like a broken record.
think: Coal closes in **2035**, so by 2039 I'd already be elsewhere.
It feels like a **good decade** for me: wiring robots or running a renewables crew.

fieldNote: He sees a decade's warning as **good news** because coal closes before robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to rebuild twice, once when the planning work goes and again when the dozers go. What would help is training on full wages and a government that treats it like an emergency.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about climate. For coal miners, AI is the second wave, not the first. Nobody should plan for one without the other.

headlineQuote: For coal miners, AI is the second wave, not the first. Nobody should plan for one without the other.
portrait: Hassan is a 27-year-old **dozer operator** at a large coal mine with a planned closure in **2035**.
He uses AI daily, runs a **drone survey** side business and has nine months saved plus an index fund.
He lives with Ama, an environmental scientist, and backs the **end of coal** himself.
He's calm in Steady Disruption but anxious in AGI by 2028, which forces **two reinventions**.
Longer timelines line up with his **exit plan** into electrical work and renewables inspection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to rebuild twice, first his survey work, then the dozer.
whatWouldHelp: Training on **full wages**, with government treating it like an **emergency**.
